title: How to Learn Terraform (Without Copy-Pasting Modules You Don't Understand)
summary:
You find a Stack Overflow answer with an aws_s3_bucket block, paste it into main.tf, run terraform apply, and it works. Two weeks later someone asks why the state file lives in that backend, or what a data source is doing in the module you copied, and you stare at the HCL like it's a foreign language again.

That pattern is how a lot of people "learn" Terraform. Snippets get you a green plan once. They don't leave you with a model you can reuse when the next stack looks different.

What actually sticks

Terraform rewards concepts more than memorized blocks. If you can explain these in plain language, most tutorials stop feeling like noise:

Providers are how Terraform talks to a platform. The AWS provider is not "AWS itself." It's the plugin that maps your HCL to AWS APIs. Wrong provider version or missing credentials usually show up before you ever touch a resource.

Resources create and manage things. Data sources read existing things. Mixing them up is a classic beginner trip: you declare a new VPC when you meant to look up the one that already exists. When I got that wrong the first time, plan happily offered to build a second network I did not want.

State is Terraform's memory of what it thinks it owns. Local state is fine for a solo sandbox. Remote state (S3, Terraform Cloud, whatever your team uses) matters the moment two people run apply, or a CI job needs the same map of reality. Lose track of state and you get "resource already exists" errors that feel personal.

plan is the preview. apply is the commit. Treat plan as the place you catch drift and typos. I still read the plan line by line on anything that touches IAM or networking.

Modules are reusable packages of resources. Variables go in; outputs come out. A module you don't understand is a black box that will surprise you in production. Copying a "best practice" VPC module with twenty variables you never open is how you ship something you can't debug at 2 a.m.

Those ideas travel. Exact argument names change between provider versions. The mental model does not.

A practice loop that beats tutorial bingeing

Pick one tiny stack. My favorite starter is an S3 bucket plus a locked-down IAM policy that can read it. No Kubernetes. No multi-account org chart. One bucket, one role or user, one outputs block that prints the bucket ARN.

Write the HCL yourself from the provider docs, not from a GitHub gist. Use terraform init, then plan, then apply. Break something on purpose: rename the bucket, change a tag, remove a required argument. Read the error. Fix it. Run plan again.

That loop teaches more than three hours of watching someone else type. You feel how state tracks the rename. You see why a force-new argument wants to destroy and recreate. You learn that terraform destroy is a tool, not a moral failure, in a throwaway account.

When a HashiCorp tutorial or a talk finally makes remote state or module composition click, save that page or video somewhere you'll reopen. Don't leave it in a browser tab named "terraform stuff (final)." Tabs die. So do bookmark folders named "infra."

Keep the learning from vanishing

Infrastructure knowledge fades between projects. You ship one stack, spend a month on app code, then blank on backends or how you wired outputs between modules.

Passive re-reading of the same intro guide feels productive and still leaves you stuck when plan shows a destroy you didn't expect. What helps is retrieval: close the docs and ask yourself what state stores, why a data source isn't a resource, and what terraform import is for. Wrong answers point at the fuzzy edge.

I park the explanations that unlocked hard parts in Recl. Share a docs page, YouTube walkthrough, or conference talk into it, get a short summary and key takeaways, drop a one-line "your note" in my own words, and let spaced recall nudges bring the idea back days later. For Terraform you only touch in bursts, that reminder matters more than the first save. The Chrome extension (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+S) helps when you're deep in provider docs and don't want to leave the tab.

Any system that captures the explanation and schedules a revisit works. Spaced repetition fits backends and providers the same way it fits flashcards, including the difference between count and for_each that you swear you'll remember next time.

Build a one-page cheat sheet you own

After your first working stack, write a short page that is yours:

Where state lives for this project, and who may apply. Which provider versions you pinned. The pattern you use for variables vs locals. How you name resources so plan is readable. The one module you'll reuse, and the rule that you must open it before you call it.

Keep it short. Next project, open that page before a new tutorial. You'll still check docs for quirks. You won't rebuild the whole model from a half-remembered gist.

Update the sheet when something surprises you. "This bucket argument became force-new in provider 5.x" saves an afternoon later. Keep those notes next to the tutorials you saved, and asking your library "what's my pattern for remote state?" beats digging through old Slack threads. Recl's ask-your-library feature is built for that; a well-tagged folder in any tool still beats scattered screenshots.

A loop you can repeat

  1. Learn the concepts once: provider, resource vs data, state, plan vs apply, modules, variables/outputs.
  2. Build one ugly stack end to end in a throwaway account.
  3. Break it, read the plan, fix it.
  4. Save the explanations that unlocked the hard parts, in your own words.
  5. Before the next infra change, quiz yourself instead of paste-searching Stack Overflow first.

Terraform isn't hard because HCL is weird. It's hard because the gaps between real uses are long, and copy-paste fills those gaps with code you can't explain. Close the gaps on purpose, and the next terraform plan stops feeling like a coin flip.

title: Promotion Between Environments as a Pull Request: A Security Review, Not a Slogan
summary:
A fintech team in Austin ships a fix on a Friday afternoon. Staging looks fine. Someone runs a manual script against production, or clicks a deploy button that pulls from a branch nobody fully diffed, and twenty minutes later the payments service is returning 500s. The post-incident question is always the same: who approved this, and what exactly got promoted? Too often the honest answer is a Slack thread, not an audit record.

This is not a tooling gap most teams lack the discipline to fix on their own. It is a design gap. If promotion between environments is a script, a manual copy, or a deploy button with no diff attached, there is no artifact to review before the fact and nothing durable to inspect after. The fix is architectural: make promotion a pull request, with the same review surface, the same CI gates, and the same revert path as any other code change.

Why promotion-as-PR is an architecture decision, not a label

Corporate AI 365 models dev, staging, and production as real git branches inside your existing GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps repository. Promoting a change from staging to production is not a separate deployment tool with its own permission model — it is a pull request from the staging branch into the production branch, reviewed and merged the same way any feature PR is.

That has consequences worth stress-testing in a security review. First, the diff is the single source of truth about what is being promoted — not a deploy log, not a changelog someone wrote by hand. Second, every gate (Developer, QA, approval, production) maps to a real git event and a permission check, so the audit trail is the commit history itself, not a side table that can drift from reality. Third, revert is symmetric: because production state is a branch, rolling back a bad release is reverting a merge commit, not improvising a hotfix under pressure.

The honest trade-off is that this only works if your branching strategy can actually represent environment state cleanly. Teams with messy, long-lived feature branches or unscripted manual hotfixes to production will feel friction here — and that friction is doing its job. It is surfacing a process gap that a deploy button was previously hiding.

Root cause without a live database connection

None of this matters if the diagnosis feeding the pull request is wrong, and diagnosis is where most AI-assisted tooling quietly asks for more access than it should. Corporate AI 365 reasons over your source code and a scripted database schema — tables, columns, constraints you export yourself — never a live connection string, never production rows. It never hosts your code either; it reads what your connector exposes and nothing else persists outside that read.

When a plain-language report — checkout is charging the wrong tax rate for Texas orders — genuinely needs live data to confirm, the system does not reach for the database itself. It writes a read-only query and hands it to your own developer to run. The result never comes back to us. That boundary is deliberate, not a limitation we are apologizing for: a platform that never touches your database cannot leak your database, and that single sentence tends to end the access-control section of a security review early.

Diagnosis is also reproducible. The same issue text against the same code snapshot and the same model produces the same root cause, confidence score, and proposed fix, because the analysis is cached against a hash of those three inputs. That matters for the approval gate specifically: QA and a manager are approving a deterministic claim, not re-running a dice roll and hoping it matches what the developer saw an hour earlier.

What this buys a lean North American team

Two pressures compound for engineering leaders across North America right now. Production downtime is expensive in a way that is easy to underestimate until it happens — industry research from ITIC puts the median cost of downtime for large enterprises at roughly $9,000 per minute, and even teams well below that scale feel the same shape of pain on a smaller multiplier. At the same time, senior engineering talent capable of tracing a production incident to a specific file and line under pressure is genuinely scarce; the skills-gap pattern documented globally — a majority of firms in some regions reporting they cannot find qualified developers — shows up in North American hiring pipelines as longer open-req times and backlogs that senior engineers simply cannot clear fast enough.

Corporate AI 365 does not remove the need for engineering judgment. It narrows the distance between a plain-language problem report and a reviewable fix, so a non-technical employee in support or operations can file what they see, and a smaller engineering team can triage, diagnose, and route the fix through governed gates without pulling a senior engineer off a roadmap item for every incident. The Employee console takes the report in plain language; the Developer and QA consoles carry the diagnosis through branches and pull requests; the Manager console and Face Off scoring make the resulting work visible and attributable — to a developer, a team, or a department — without guesswork about who actually closed the loop.

For a company whose production minutes are expensive and whose senior hires are hard to find, that is the practical case for treating environment promotion as a pull request: not a workflow preference, but a control that a security review, a QA lead, and a CFO can all sign off on for the same reasons.

title: Picking an MDM in 2026: Jamf, NinjaOne, JumpCloud and the Apple-versus-everything question
summary:
According to IDC data, the average enterprise now manages more than 10,000 endpoint devices, and 60% of that fleet is mobile. Every one of those devices is a potential compliance gap, a lost-laptop incident, or an unpatched app away from a real problem. G2 evaluated more than 20 MDM platforms against its Spring 2026 Grid Report to find the nine that actually hold up once you're managing that many endpoints instead of just a handful. Here's where they land, and the decision that shapes almost everything else: do you go all-in on Apple, or build for whatever shows up on the network.

Jamf is the Apple-only pick, and it earns that position with an 86% ease-of-setup score on G2. Zero-touch deployment through Apple Business Manager means a new MacBook configures itself, installs security settings, and deploys required apps the moment it's unboxed — no manual setup. Jamf also scores 94% on Apple Support, backed by deep scripting support (Bash, Python) for workflows standard MDM policies don't cover. The tradeoff is total: Jamf doesn't support Windows or Android at all, so any mixed-device org needs a second tool alongside it. Pricing starts at $5.75 per device per month, billed annually.

NinjaOne is the MSP-style remote endpoint pick, built as a hybrid MDM-RMM rather than a dedicated mobile tool. It posts a 94% ease-of-setup score and a 94% Ease of Admin score on G2, with an agent-based system that auto-enrolls devices the moment the agent installs. Its built-in third-party patching (Zoom, Chrome, Adobe, not just OS-level updates) is a differentiator reviewers call out repeatedly. The honest gap: mobile policy enforcement is noticeably thinner than its desktop controls — encryption and passcode enforcement work, but app management and containerization don't exist yet. Pricing is custom, quoted per endpoint.

JumpCloud is the cloud-native identity-plus-device pick, and it's less an MDM than a full identity, device, and security platform. Over 90% of G2 reviewers say they'd recommend it to another IT team, and it posts a 91% multi-systems support rating for tying SSO, MFA, MDM, and directory services into one console. That identity integration is the real draw — provisioning and de-provisioning sync directly with HR tools. The tradeoff: mobile app management isn't granular (no real containerization), and enrolling iOS/Android devices sometimes needs manual re-enrollment after OS updates. Free tier available; paid plans start at $3 per user per month.

Admin, Google's MDM, is the lightweight cross-platform pick for SMBs that don't need enterprise complexity. It posts a 93% applications management rating and a 90% usage-information score on G2, with flexible enrollment (QR codes, email invites, bulk CSV, ABM, Android Zero-Touch) and useful device-usage analytics beyond just security metrics. The gap: real-time device-level diagnostics are limited, and there's no multi-tiered admin role structure for larger IT teams. Pricing is custom.

Iru, formerly Kandji, is the second Apple-only pick, distinguished by auto-remediation: it continuously monitors devices and fixes compliance drift without IT stepping in. It posts a 94% ease-of-setup score and a 95% Ease of Admin score on G2, the highest admin-experience rating of the Apple-focused tools, plus 150+ pre-built Blueprints mapped to CIS, SOC 2, ISO 27001, and NIST. Like Jamf, it's Apple-exclusive — mixed Windows environments need a second platform. Pricing is custom, based on device count.

AirDroid Business is the Android field-operations pick, built for fleets of tablets, kiosks, POS systems, and rugged devices rather than office laptops. It posts a 98% ease-of-admin score — the highest of any tool in this list — and a 98% quality-of-support score, with kiosk-mode customization and real-time device health monitoring (CPU, storage, battery) without physical access. It now supports Windows alongside Android, though iOS and macOS remain unsupported entirely. Pricing starts at $2.97 per device per month.

Rippling IT takes the unified HR-and-IT approach: device provisioning is tied directly to the employee lifecycle, so a new hire's laptop, apps, and access configure automatically, and offboarding revokes everything in the same workflow. It posts a 95% meets-requirements score and an 89% average user adoption rate on G2. The tradeoff: MDM-specific depth lags dedicated tools, since feature requests compete with core HR priorities. Pricing is custom, based on modules selected.

TeamViewer earns its spot on remote access rather than policy depth — a 95% multi-systems support score on G2 reflects how reliably it works across Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android, even on weak connections. HIPAA-compliant encryption and MFA make it viable for regulated remote support. But its MDM controls are genuinely thin: no app-level restrictions, no geofencing, no zero-trust framework. Pricing starts at $24.90 per month for remote access.

IBM MaaS360 is the AI-powered enterprise pick, using Watson for proactive risk scoring and real-time threat detection across iOS, Android, Windows, and macOS from one console. It posts an 86% meets-requirements score and an 89% regulation-compliant rating on G2, with secure containerization that reviewers in healthcare and finance call a compliance necessity. The consistent complaint: the admin interface feels dated, with settings buried in extra clicks. Pricing runs $5 per device per user.

The Apple-versus-everything question actually answers itself once you look at the fleet: if the org is Apple-only, Jamf and Iru both outperform anything cross-platform on depth, and Iru's auto-remediation makes it the lower-maintenance of the two. The moment Windows, Android, or a mixed BYOD policy enters the picture, JumpCloud's identity-plus-device model or NinjaOne's hybrid MDM-RMM approach cover more ground than forcing an Apple-only tool to do something it wasn't built for.

Full scoring breakdown, the complete comparison table, and G2's evaluation criteria across all nine tools are here: Best MDM Solutions for 2026: 9 Tools Worth Considering.

title: Your build attestation is a chain of custody, not a safety certificate
summary:
Picture a release with a perfect paper trail. You have the reviewed commit, the resolved dependencies, the builder identity, the artifact digest, and a green record of every check that ran. All of it is signed.

It can still contain a bug that lets anyone mark an invoice as paid.

Provenance is worth having, and AI-assisted development makes it more useful, because teams increasingly need to reconstruct how a change came together. The trouble starts when a complete record begins to feel like evidence that the code is good.

The audit trail vs. the actual behavior

Provenance answers questions like these:

  • Which commit is in this artifact?
  • Who approved it?
  • Which dependency versions were resolved?
  • Which build produced it, and which checks ran?

Those answers are valuable during an incident, and they help you reproduce a release. None of them tells you whether the code does the right thing.

The scenarios below are illustrative, not real incidents.

Failure mode 1: faithfully recording the wrong code

An assistant helps write a payment webhook:

app.post("/webhooks/payments", (req, res) => {
  const sig = req.get("X-Signature");
  if (sig && !verifySignature(req.rawBody, sig)) {
    return res.sendStatus(401);
  }
  markInvoicePaid(req.body.invoiceId);
  res.sendStatus(200);
});

A bad signature gets rejected. A request with no signature at all skips the check and marks the invoice paid.

The build can be hermetic and the attestation can verify cleanly. The record is accurate: this exact code, built this exact way, reached production. Build integrity tells you the artifact wasn't tampered with on the way there, and frameworks like SLSA are aimed at that problem. Whether the source was right to begin with is a separate question.

Failure mode 2: "checks ran" gets read as "checks were enough"

The tests for that webhook might cover a valid signature and an invalid one. Both pass, so the record says unit-tests: pass, and that's true.

The missing case is the one that matters:

test("rejects a webhook with no signature", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)
    .post("/webhooks/payments")
    .send({ invoiceId: "inv_123" });
  expect(res.status).toBe(401);
});

A provenance record can show that a job ran and passed. It can't show what the job never tried.

Failure mode 3: a record of review isn't a record of scrutiny

approved_by: reviewer-a is a fact about a click. It doesn't tell you whether the reviewer traced the unsigned path, or spent four minutes on a large AI-assisted diff near the end of the day.

Keep the approval record. Just don't let it stand in for the review itself. On sensitive changes, the reviewer should be able to answer a specific question: what happens when this header is missing?

Failure mode 4: a clean scan is a snapshot

A dependency scan can pass on release day, and a vulnerability in one of those packages can be published a week later. The record of that clean scan stays true while the risk changes.

Here, provenance earns its keep. If you recorded exactly what shipped, you can answer "are we affected?" in minutes instead of guessing. Just treat the old scan result as a dated observation, and keep scanning what's already deployed.

Failure mode 5: the audit log becomes the leak

It's tempting to capture everything an AI tool touched, including full prompts. But prompts pick up whatever a developer pasted in: a stack trace with a customer's email address, a production log, a connection string.

Now that material sits in a long-lived record that may be widely readable, kept in the name of traceability.

Most incident questions don't need the raw prompt. Something like this usually goes a long way:

{
  "artifact_digest": "sha256:...",
  "commit": "9f3c1ab",
  "pull_request": 4821,
  "approved_by": ["reviewer-a"],
  "lockfile_sha256": "...",
  "builder": "ci/release.yml@refs/tags/v2.14.0",
  "checks": [
    { "name": "unit-tests", "result": "pass" },
    { "name": "static-analysis", "tool_version": "...", "result": "pass" }
  ],
  "ai_assisted": true,
  "ai_tool": "assistant-name@version"
}

That shape is only an example. If you want a standard format, look at SLSA provenance and in-toto attestations. If your team does need to keep prompts, redact them, limit who can read them, and give them a retention period.

What goes in the record, and what still has to happen

Record what helps you explain and reproduce a release:

  • Commit, PR, and approvers
  • Resolved dependencies
  • Builder identity and artifact digest
  • Which checks ran, with tool versions and results
  • Whether AI tools were involved, and which ones

Then do the work the record can't do for you:

  • Code review: is this the right behavior?
  • Testing: does it do what the requirement says, including what it has to refuse?
  • Security analysis: are there risky patterns, data flows, vulnerable dependencies, or committed secrets?

Provenance is the part that lets you trace and reproduce a release. Those three are how you find out whether it should have shipped.

A signed record tells you where the software came from. It takes a different kind of work to know whether it's safe.

What does your team actually record for AI-assisted changes, and has any of it helped you during a real incident? Do you keep prompts, or did you decide against it?

title: SaaS sprawl is a finance problem engineers create. Here is what spend tools fix.
summary:
Every engineering team has a version of this story: someone spins up a trial to solve a problem on a Tuesday, it works well enough to stick, and eighteen months later finance finds a $400/month subscription nobody remembers approving. Multiply that by every team in the org and you get the thing nobody budgeted for — SaaS sprawl.

G2 evaluated more than 20 SaaS spend management platforms against its Grid Report data to find the ones that actually fix this instead of just dashboarding it. According to that data, the average user adoption rate for SaaS spend management software sits at 63% — a genuinely strong number that suggests these tools get used, not shelved after onboarding. Here's where seven of them land.

Vertice is the mid-market and enterprise procurement pick, used by 85% mid-market companies according to G2 data. It gives teams a database of 16,000+ vendor pricing benchmarks and pairs it with dedicated procurement specialists, so negotiations run on comparable data instead of guesswork. Reviewers consistently call out the clean dashboard and the hands-on support team, which functions less like a vendor and more like an extension of your own procurement org. Pricing is custom.

SpendHound is the budget-conscious pick, and the standout detail is that it's 100% free — a rarity in this category. It's used by 77% mid-market and 23% small-business teams, who get an automated renewal dashboard, negotiation support, and real-time pricing benchmarks without a subscription fee attached. The honest tradeoff: G2 reviewers note it's intentionally lightweight on advanced reporting and customization, which is the same simplicity that makes it fast to adopt.

Mesh Payments is the real-time visibility pick — the one a pure cost-tracking list easily misses, but G2's own evaluation ranks it third overall. It gives finance teams live transaction visibility and virtual or physical corporate cards with per-vendor spend limits, so a card can be frozen or canceled instantly rather than chased down after the fact. Reviewers highlight automated receipt capture and streamlined approval workflows as the features that cut the most manual work. Pricing starts at $10 per user per month.

Cledara is the centralized-monitoring pick for finance teams, used by about 57% mid-market and 42% small-business teams per G2 data. It consolidates every SaaS subscription into one dashboard with built-in approval workflows and virtual cards that can be killed instantly when someone leaves the company. The tradeoff reviewers mention most: accounting integrations aren't universal, so some teams still do light manual CSV work. Pricing runs £75 per month.

Spendbase is the company-wide expense-tracking pick, used by 62% mid-market and 38% small-business teams. What sets it apart isn't just visibility — it's that Spendbase charges only 25% of the savings it actually finds, which ties its revenue directly to results instead of a flat subscription. Reviewers praise the vendor usage insights that make renewal and consolidation decisions easier, though some want deeper dashboard customization. Pricing is custom.

Flexera One is the large-enterprise pick, with 74% of its users coming from large organizations managing complex IT environments. It unifies visibility across on-premise, cloud, and SaaS assets in one place, and its license reconciliation feature is frequently cited as a direct source of savings by catching unused seats before renewal. The honest cost: reviewers describe a real learning curve and note the platform is a bigger investment, one enterprise teams say pays for itself through the depth of control it provides. Pricing is custom.

Tropic is the data-driven procurement pick for teams managing large vendor lists, with around 86% mid-market adoption according to G2. It centralizes benchmark insights, vendor negotiations, contract management, and invoice matching in one workflow, with custom approval chains that keep finance, legal, and security looped in on every purchase. Reviewers flag that OCR-based contract extraction sometimes needs manual review, which the vendor treats as an active area of refinement. Pricing is custom.

One correction worth flagging: the brief for this piece named six of these tools but left out Mesh Payments, which G2's own evaluation actually ranks third overall in its seven best SaaS spend management software for 2026. It's included above because leaving it out would understate the real-time visibility category entirely.

None of these tools solve SaaS sprawl by existing. They solve it when a team actually uses the visibility they provide to ask "why are we still paying for this" before the renewal, not after. Vertice and Tropic lean into procurement and negotiation, SpendHound and Cledara win on accessibility and centralization, Mesh Payments and Spendbase tie spend directly to real-time control and savings, and Flexera One exists for the enterprises where the SaaS stack is really an IT asset problem wearing a finance hat.

Full scoring breakdown, the complete tool-by-tool comparison, and G2's evaluation methodology are here: My 7 Best SaaS Spend Management Software Picks for 2026.

title: Deploying AI Models Explained: Versions, Canaries and Drift
summary:
A team deploys a new version of the AI model behind its support agent, the one that handles refunds. The new version passes every test. On five hundred old conversations it gets the right answer ninety one times in a hundred, and the old version gets eighty seven. So on Tuesday, every conversation goes to the new version.

Everything looks fine. Latency is 410 ms, errors are zero, every health check is green and every trace is complete.

A week later, the team reviews the refunds the agent approved. One in every eight was wrong. The month before, it was one in forty. The agent had been confidently approving refunds it should have refused, and nothing had ever errored.

This article follows that week back to its causes, and ends with the three habits that would have caught it. The video tells the same story in six minutes. This is the written version.

Which model answered this?

The first question was simple. Which model gave these answers? Nobody could say.

Every log line said the model was latest:

{"time":"19:41:02","order_id":"4473","decision":"refund approved","model":"latest"}

But latest is not a version. It just means whichever version is newest today. The team's config asked for latest, so on Tuesday it got the new version, and on the day the vendor moves the name again, it will get another one without anyone deciding it. The vendor named the exact version in every reply, support-v2-0917, and nobody had logged it.

A model is a file of numbers. Nobody wrote those numbers, so you cannot read them to find out what changed. The only way to tell one model from another is its version. That gives two rules:

agent:
  model: support-v2-0917   # pin the exact version, never a moving name like "latest"

{"time":"19:41:02","order_id":"4473","decision":"refund approved",
 "model_requested":"support-v2-0917","model_answered":"support-v2-0917"}

Pin the exact version in your config. And in every log line, write down the version that actually answered, taken from the response, not the one you asked for. Many model APIs accept a moving name and tell you in each response which exact version answered, so the field is there for you to log.

The tests only proved the past

The tests passed, so how could the model be wrong?

Because those five hundred conversations were from last month. The model was graded on the past.

Code is tested against rules, and rules don't change. If a function returned the right total last month, it returns the right total today. A model is tested against real conversations, and those keep changing. A score on last month's conversations tells you how the model would have done last month.

So a passing score doesn't mean you can send the model to everyone. It means the model is ready to meet real customers, a few at a time.

Shadow: run the new model beside the old one

Here's what careful teams do first. Run the new model beside the old one. The customer still gets the old model's answer. The new model's answer goes only into a log.

Answer answer = oldModel.answer(conversation);             // the customer gets this one
shadowPool.submit(() ->                                     // the new model answers too, off the request path
    shadowLog.write(conversation.id(), answer, newModel.answer(conversation)));
return answer;

After a day you have thousands of answers from both, and you read the ones where they disagree. Most pairs will match. The ones that differ, the old model refusing where the new one approves, are exactly the refunds the review found a week too late.

Shadow runs cost a second model call while they run, so most teams run them for a day or two, or on a sample of the traffic.

Canary: five conversations in a hundred

Then the new model answers for real, but only for five conversations in a hundred. That's a canary.

// The same conversation always lands on the same side, so a customer never switches model in the middle of a chat.
boolean useNew = Math.floorMod(conversationId.hashCode(), 100) < canaryPercent;   // 5, then 25, 50, 100
String model = useNew ? config.newModel() : config.oldModel();

You watch those five closely: how often the model approves a refund, and how often someone asks for a human. Compare them with the other ninety five over the same hours, so the time of day and the kind of customer match. If anything looks wrong, only five customers in a hundred saw it.

Widen it, or roll it back

If those five hold up, give the new model a quarter of the conversations, then half, then all of them.

And if it goes wrong, rolling back is one line. You point the config back at the previous version, or set the canary to zero. That only works if you know which version you were on, which is the first habit again.

A passing score earns a model a canary, not every customer.

Drift: it gets worse, and nothing errors

Suppose the team does all of that. The model can still go wrong slowly, and not one error will appear. That's drift.

The customers change. A festival sale brings new buyers who ask things last month's customers never asked. The model keeps answering just as confidently, because it only knows last month's customers. In the story, the share of refunds it approves sits at thirty percent for weeks, then creeps to forty five percent over seven days. Every health check stays green the whole time.

You can't catch drift with an error rate, because nothing errors.

Watch two numbers, then check the truth

There is a second problem: the truth arrives late. You only learn whether a refund was right a week later, at the review.

So you watch in two layers. Every hour, you watch two numbers: how often the model approves, and how often people ask for a human. They are not the truth, but they move first.

SELECT date_trunc('hour', created_at)                                     AS hour,
       model_answered,
       avg(CASE WHEN decision = 'refund approved' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)    AS approve_rate,
       avg(CASE WHEN asked_for_human THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)                 AS human_rate
FROM agent_decisions
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

And when the review comes, you check those numbers against the truth. If the approval rate climbed in the same week the wrong refunds climbed, the hourly number was the early warning, and next time you act on it sooner.

The law

A model passes its tests on the past. Pin its version, roll it out slowly, and keep checking it against the truth.

How real teams do it

None of this is new to teams that ship models every week.

  • Uber checks a new model against past production data before release, runs shadow tests in more than 75 percent of its critical online use cases, starts every rollout on a small slice of traffic, and rolls back automatically when failure signals appear: Raising the Bar on ML Model Deployment Safety (Uber Engineering, 2025).
  • DoorDash logs every prediction with the versioned name of the model that made it, and checks the statistics of those predictions every hour: Maintaining Machine Learning Model Accuracy Through Monitoring (DoorDash Engineering, 2021).

Both write about trained models, not only about large language models. The habits are the same.

Next time

We go inside the database and watch what happens to a row the moment you write it.

The support agent, the refunds, the scores and the version names are an invented example. What is the last thing you shipped that passed every test and still went wrong?

Here's what careful teams do first. Run the new model beside the old one. The customer still gets the old model's answer. The new model's answer goes only into a log.

Answer answer = oldModel.answer(conversation);             // the customer gets this one
shadowPool.submit(() ->                                     // the new model answers too, off the request path
    shadowLog.write(conversation.id(), answer, newModel.answer(conversation)));
return answer;

After a day you have thousands of answers from both, and you read the ones where they disagree. Most pairs will match. The ones that differ, the old model refusing where the new one approves, are exactly the refunds the review found a week too late.

Shadow runs cost a second model call while they run, so most teams run them for a day or two, or on a sample of the traffic.

Canary: five conversations in a hundred

Then the new model answers for real, but only for five conversations in a hundred. That's a canary.

// The same conversation always lands on the same side, so a customer never switches model in the middle of a chat.
boolean useNew = Math.floorMod(conversationId.hashCode(), 100) < canaryPercent;   // 5, then 25, 50, 100
String model = useNew ? config.newModel() : config.oldModel();

You watch those five closely: how often the model approves a refund, and how often someone asks for a human. Compare them with the other ninety five over the same hours, so the time of day and the kind of customer match. If anything looks wrong, only five customers in a hundred saw it.

Widen it, or roll it back

If those five hold up, give the new model a quarter of the conversations, then half, then all of them.

And if it goes wrong, rolling back is one line. You point the config back at the previous version, or set the canary to zero. That only works if you know which version you were on, which is the first habit again.

A passing score earns a model a canary, not every customer.

Drift: it gets worse, and nothing errors

Suppose the team does all of that. The model can still go wrong slowly, and not one error will appear. That's drift.

The customers change. A festival sale brings new buyers who ask things last month's customers never asked. The model keeps answering just as confidently, because it only knows last month's customers. In the story, the share of refunds it approves sits at thirty percent for weeks, then creeps to forty five percent over seven days. Every health check stays green the whole time.

You can't catch drift with an error rate, because nothing errors.

Watch two numbers, then check the truth

There is a second problem: the truth arrives late. You only learn whether a refund was right a week later, at the review.

So you watch in two layers. Every hour, you watch two numbers: how often the model approves, and how often people ask for a human. They are not the truth, but they move first.

SELECT date_trunc('hour', created_at)                                     AS hour,
       model_answered,
       avg(CASE WHEN decision = 'refund approved' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)    AS approve_rate,
       avg(CASE WHEN asked_for_human THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)                 AS human_rate
FROM agent_decisions
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

And when the review comes, you check those numbers against the truth. If the approval rate climbed in the same week the wrong refunds climbed, the hourly number was the early warning, and next time you act on it sooner.

The law

A model passes its tests on the past. Pin its version, roll it out slowly, and keep checking it against the truth.

How real teams do it

None of this is new to teams that ship models every week.

  • Uber checks a new model against past production data before release, runs shadow tests in more than 75 percent of its critical online use cases, starts every rollout on a small slice of traffic, and rolls back automatically when failure signals appear: Raising the Bar on ML Model Deployment Safety (Uber Engineering, 2025).
  • DoorDash logs every prediction with the versioned name of the model that made it, and checks the statistics of those predictions every hour: Maintaining Machine Learning Model Accuracy Through Monitoring (DoorDash Engineering, 2021).

Both write about trained models, not only about large language models. The habits are the same.

Next time

We go inside the database and watch what happens to a row the moment you write it.

The support agent, the refunds, the scores and the version names are an invented example. What is the last thing you shipped that passed every test and still went wrong?

title: Calculating your Company's Required DevOps Capacity

This article was written by Michael Zion, CEO at MeteorOps, and first published on the MeteorOps blog.

The capacity conversation usually starts after the workaround breaks

A client recently asked the platform-engineering question that shows up when a company has grown past the “one senior engineer keeps delivery moving through heroics” stage. A handful of deployment scripts had turned into the operating layer for engineering: CI/CD workflows, cloud account and project structure, Kubernetes and serverless deployment paths, infrastructure-as-code modules, runtime standards, incident support, security guardrails, cost controls, secrets and access patterns, and the enablement work that stops teams from losing days to broken environments, unclear ownership, or knowledge trapped in chat threads.

The budget question was direct: why does this environment need three DevOps engineers instead of one? The useful answer is not “because DevOps is important.” It is capacity math. Start with committed roadmap work, then add the operational load that rarely fits neatly into sprint planning: production escalations, pull request reviews, Terraform drift, failed pipelines, certificate and dependency updates, audit evidence, cost investigations, access requests, policy exceptions, flaky test infrastructure, base image patching, and the steady stream of “quick” developer support. In 2026, that background load is often heavier than the original platform plan assumed: more AI-assisted code reaching review, more short-lived environments, more compliance evidence, more cloud spend scrutiny, and more security checks pushed into the delivery path. If one engineer is expected to review infrastructure changes, unblock releases, tune cluster policies, handle on-call escalations, prepare audit artifacts, investigate cloud spend, and coach product teams through platform changes, staffing is no longer a preference debate. It is a business decision about how much delivery delay, burnout, single-point-of-failure risk, and platform instability the company is willing to carry in the system that ships and runs its software.

Until that moment, the budget conversation had been relatively easy.

If storage utilization is climbing, you can show the graph and justify another few hundred dollars a month for disks.

If CI queues are delaying merges, deployments still require hand-holding, cloud accounts have weak guardrails, incidents are pulling senior engineers out of roadmap work, and product teams are waiting days for platform fixes, the case is harder to express. You are not buying “1.5 DevOps engineers”; you are buying release throughput, operational safety, faster recovery, cost control, compliance readiness, and fewer blocked engineers across the company.

That is the gap these capacity formulas are meant to close. They take symptoms that usually arrive as scattered complaints — slow deployments, rising incident load, a platform backlog that never shrinks, fragile environments, security and compliance requests, cloud cost surprises, and constant support interruptions — and turn them into planning inputs that engineering, product, and finance can discuss without relying on the loudest anecdote in the room.

🛠️ Practical enough for planning, honest about uncertainty

Use the formulas below as planning heuristics, not as a precise model of human work and not as a staffing ratio to copy from another company. A five-team SaaS business, a regulated enterprise, and a small product group built mostly on managed cloud services will make different assumptions about ownership, risk, automation, on-call coverage, compliance effort, lead time, and how much platform complexity they are willing to operate themselves.

The point is not to produce a magic number. The point is to make the constraints visible: where operational pressure is coming from, which teams are absorbing it, which roadmap work is being delayed, and what tradeoff the business is making if it chooses not to hire, reduce scope, standardize tooling, improve self-service, retire complexity, or simplify the platform. A useful capacity model should make the next decision clearer, even if the number is still an estimate.

I call these formulas because they create a repeatable way to reason about capacity, not because engineering work can be measured with mathematical precision.

DevOps and platform work is shaped by interruptions, context switching, unclear ownership, production risk, and organizational friction. A useful model has to be simple enough for engineering managers, platform leads, and executives to use together, while still being honest enough to show where the pressure is really coming from.

Decisions this capacity model should help you make

  1. Help you understand how many DevOps Engineers you need

  2. Provide you with tools to reason with your CFO

  3. Encourage you to learn martial arts to successfully defeat your CFO in combat if all else fails

🤷 Caveats

  1. This model is not written in stone; I’m open to learning from your experience and improving it based on what you see in real engineering organizations.

  2. Calibrate the formulas before using the result

  3. Most of the formulas use inputs you can count: developers, services, environments, pipelines, incidents, and support channels. Those numbers are useful, but they do not explain the whole capacity picture. Qualitative factors such as ownership clarity, automation coverage, documentation quality, supportability, and maintenance debt can change the real capacity requirement as much as raw volume does. Ten services with consistent deployment patterns may be easier to support than three services with bespoke pipelines, unclear runbooks, and no obvious owner.

  4. DevOps capacity is not the same as one full-time DevOps engineer

Use the formulas without fooling yourself

  1. Start by identifying what your current DevOps capacity can reliably support, then treat that as the baseline unit. For example:

    160 hours of DevOps engineering per month = 20 microservices, 3 development teams, a defined release cadence, a known incident load, and a specific amount of platform support.

    The variables will differ by company, and the numbers only matter if they reflect real work. The point is to stop treating “one DevOps engineer” as a generic planning unit and instead measure the operating load that a given amount of capacity is carrying.

  2. As the company grows, look for indicators the existing capacity isn’t able to handle more than it does and hire more DevOps capacity

🚨 The indicators that more DevOps capacity is required

There are 2 main indicators that more DevOps capacity is required:

  1. Support work is useful until it becomes the platform interface.

    Some support load is healthy. When the company is growing, the queue often shows where developers are getting stuck: unclear deployment paths, missing documentation, brittle environments, confusing access flows, or platform defaults that do not match real use.

    The failure mode is different. If the same questions, access requests, deployment failures, and environment fixes keep coming back, support has stopped being discovery. It has become capacity leakage. At that point, DevOps-to-developer efficiency improves only when recurring support is converted into self-service, safer defaults, clearer ownership, or automation that removes the ticket altogether.

  2. Different engineers and teams are solving the same problems in different ways for themselves.

    This often starts when DevOps or platform hiring lags behind demand and developers cannot wait for every environment, pipeline, permission, or deployment issue to be handled centrally. Some local problem-solving is healthy, but it becomes expensive when every team builds its own scripts, Terraform patterns, CI templates, dashboards, or access workflows in isolation.

    It is acceptable for product teams to solve DevOps use cases when those solutions become contributions to a shared platform or a documented standard. It is a warning sign when the same problem is being solved five different ways and none of those solutions are reusable, supportable, or owned.

Example client indicators:

  1. Company #1 example:

    A company with roughly 300 developers had about 40 DevOps engineers spread across stateless infrastructure, data infrastructure, monitoring, CI/CD, and data streaming. Each group owned a Slack support channel. Over time, those channels became the default front door for pipeline failures, infrastructure questions, access requests, environment issues, and production follow-ups.

    Capacity signal: Several DevOps teams needed 1–3 engineers available mainly for support rotation. That was not just an on-call coverage issue. It showed that platform engineers had become a manual intake layer for work that should have been automated, documented, delegated, or exposed through self-service. The visible symptom was “too many questions in Slack”; the underlying capacity problem was that routine delivery work still required a specialist to interpret, approve, or execute it.

    What changed: The teams reviewed recurring requests every week, grouped the highest-volume patterns, automated repeatable tasks, and created self-service paths for common developer needs. They also paired with key developers to move platform knowledge into product teams. The capacity gain did not come from asking DevOps engineers to work faster. It came from removing avoidable handoffs and making routine work executable without waiting for an answer in Slack.

  2. Company #2 example:

    A company with 30 developers had one DevOps engineer supporting delivery, infrastructure, and developer requests.

    Capacity signal: The DevOps engineer spent most of their time on support tickets opened by developers. As common deployment errors kept recurring, some developers began bypassing the standard deployment process to keep work moving.

    What changed: The company added monthly capacity through a part-time DevOps consultant and trained key developers to provide first-line support inside their teams. That combination reduced the single-person bottleneck without immediately turning every platform problem into a full-time hiring decision.

With those caveats in place, here is the planning model for estimating DevOps capacity.

A practical way to estimate DevOps capacity

A useful way to estimate required DevOps capacity is to start with the work the platform team must absorb, then adjust for risk, complexity, and the level of self-service already in place:

Why this works as a planning model

  • The bigger the stuff to build and maintain - the more working hands you need

  • The more variations you need to support - the more working hands you need

  • The more self-service you have, the fewer hands-on interruptions you should need

Let’s dive into the ingredients of scale, complexity, and leverage.

The baseline: what “DevOps capacity” actually includes

The guiding principle here is simple: a DevOps engineer should enable delivery, not become a permanent checkpoint for every delivery task.

That means enabling teams to provision infrastructure, deploy workloads, store and process data, observe services, and recover from incidents with as little unnecessary handoff as possible. When every change still requires a DevOps engineer to approve, debug, click, or explain the same thing again, capacity is being consumed by friction rather than leverage.

DevOps = Enable ownership of the relevant stakeholders over the infrastructure, monitoring, security, architecture, data, configuration, deployment, orchestration, testing, and development.

‘DevOps Capacity’ is the time & effort invested in achieving “DevOps” as defined above.

⛰️ Scale - Size Matters

Start by defining the scale you are asking the platform to support. In capacity planning, “scale” is not only traffic volume. It also includes the number of services, environments, deployment paths, cloud accounts or projects, runtime patterns, data systems, compliance boundaries, and teams that depend on the platform.

“Michael, did you just create a recursive definition?”

Why yes of course! this is the rationale:

  1. Larger systems require more time and effort to understand, build, secure, operate, and maintain.

  2. Larger teams and client bases create more internal and external use cases to support, which increases the load on platform, infrastructure, and release processes.

To make the two types of scale above easier to discuss, I use two simple capacity models.

They are not scientific laws. They are structured ways to compare the demand created by your systems, teams, and operating model with the DevOps capacity your organization actually has:

Map the system scale and operational surface area

  • Resources Used could mean many things, some of them are: Storage volume, Number of CPU cores, Number of nodes, Memory used, etc.

  • System throughput is the work your systems process over time: user requests, scheduled jobs, batch runs, queue events, streaming workloads, and any other flow that creates operational load. Throughput matters because each flow tends to bring its own deployment risk, scaling pattern, observability requirement, failure mode, ownership boundary, and support expectation. A quiet batch job that fails every morning can consume more DevOps attention than a high-traffic service with mature dashboards, alerts, and rollback paths.

  • Instances per Service refers to the number of replicas of the services developed within your company, for example: Kubernetes Pods, serverless functions executions, etc.

A client's system scale example: 1-year-old startup

Scale: 3 AWS ECS clusters, 6 microservices, 3 main environments, 3–150 ephemeral development environments, and 6–40 container instances per environment

Approach: Infrastructure and deployments are managed with infrastructure as code. The company hired a part-time DevOps consultant to implement the initial system and train the development team to own routine changes, instead of creating a permanent dependency on the consultant for every deployment or environment issue.

Organization Scale

  • Number of Developers refers to the number of developers, and shame on you for bothering yourself with reading this line

  • Total Users refers to the number of active clients_

    Noteworthy:

    B2C will usually have more clients, with more standardized interfaces - DevOps Engineers most likely will be less involved in direct ways with client facing features.

    B2B on the other hand will usually have less clients, with more customized interfaces per client - DevOps Engineers are more involved with client-facing features through the developers._

A Client's Organization Scale Example - Healthcare Company:

Scale: 200 developers divided into teams of 4–12 people, 10 DevOps engineers and SREs, high autonomy per team, and no single standardized process for all developers

Approach: Infrastructure and deployments are managed with infrastructure as code to support “one-click environments.” The company also used a part-time DevOps consultant to implement an initial system and train the development team to take ownership of it.

Bonus: Check our availability for a call about scaling DevOps in your organization in a more gradual way using MeteorOps.

🥴 Complexity - More Options, Less Clarity

I know, I know… It looks similar to the chapter about Scale.

In this context, complexity is not only the number of systems you run. It is the number of choices engineers must make without strong defaults, and the uncertainty around which path is considered safe, supported, and maintainable. That uncertainty creates decision latency and makes it more likely that two teams solve the same problem in different, incompatible ways.

You are operating in a complex environment when an engineer knows what outcome they want, but still has to ask, “Is this how we do it here?”

So, what does complexity have to do with both the system and the organization?

  1. More complex system - More time and effort are required to map the available options, and customize (copy, paste, modify) or generalize (refactor, parameterize) solutions

  2. More complex organization - More time and effort are required to communicate, provide support, cascade initiatives through the company, and lower likelihood of initiatives getting accepted

This time I’ll present you with the formulas for complexity without drumrolls:

System Complexity

  • Number of Tools refers to any tool, either existing or custom-built, that helps build and maintain the system. More tools mean more capabilities, more potential integrations between tools, and more potential ways to achieve the same goals. (Tools have an upside as well!)

  • Number of Platforms means any platform on which you run workloads or consume resources (e.g. - AWS, Kubernetes, Linux, Jenkins). Using more platforms requires supporting more ways of running each workload or consuming each resource.

  • Number of Codebases refers to the repositories where your systems are developed and maintained. The more separate codebases you operate, the harder it becomes to keep development workflows consistent: build conventions drift, CI/CD pipelines fork, dependency upgrades happen unevenly, and release practices become harder to support at scale. A larger number of repositories does not automatically mean you need more DevOps capacity, but it does increase the value of shared templates, standards, and automation that prevent every team from reinventing the same delivery path.

  • Number of Services is the number of services developed by the developers: more services, more different units with different logic to them, which in turn creates more unique operational requirements.

To sum up, ‘System Complexity’ increases when there are more services, running on more platforms, managed by more tools, across more codebases.

A Client's System Complexity Example - Low Scale, High Complexity:

  • Complexity: The entire system was 1 service deployed on just 1 server, but was deployed using multiple deployment tools (chef, ansible, bash scripts), from multiple different repositories (about 10), with a specific set of steps required to fully set it up
  • Approach: Containerize everything, Consolidate the deployment to one docker-compose file, Consolidate the configuration and automation to one tool (ansible), Consolidate the repositories into one

Organization Complexity

  • Number of Teams - More teams mean supporting and maintaining more ways of work

  • Number of Hierarchy Levels - More middle-management layers in the organization make it more likely decisions and communication will cascade through it, and so increasing the time & effort for decision-making and communication

  • Level of Hierarchy-Reliance for Communication - Exactly the same effect, but focused on the culture of the company

🪄 Is there anything that makes DevOps capacity more efficient?

Calculating DevOps capacity is not just a headcount exercise. Done well, it exposes where delivery is actually getting stuck: repeated support requests, fragile release paths, manual environment provisioning, unclear ownership, noisy incident handoffs, and the morale cost of constant interruption.

The better planning question is not “how many DevOps engineers do we need?” It is “which constraint should the next unit of capacity remove?” In many organizations, adding another person to absorb tickets only makes the bottleneck quieter for a while. The higher-leverage move may be self-service environment creation, paved-road CI/CD templates, standardized cloud and Kubernetes defaults, documented escalation paths, workable access flows, or clearer ownership boundaries that show when a product team can act independently and when platform help is required. If the discussion is stuck in anecdotes, a structured DevOps maturity assessment can give teams a shared language for deciding what to automate, what to standardize, what to delegate, and where specialist DevOps or platform engineering capacity still matters. The goal is not to keep the platform team busy. It is to make the same capacity support more teams, safer releases, and faster recovery without turning that team into the permanent approval queue for every deployment, pipeline change, cloud request, access issue, or post-incident follow-up.

Valid question! And this is the formula for DevOps ‘Leverage’:

  • Documentation Coverage - Out of the internal company’s tools and processes, what percentage has documentation?

  • Automated Processes Coverage - Out of the manual processes used by the developers, what percentage was automated?

  • Engineering Talent Concentration Score - The seniority (relevant experience) of your engineering team, divided by the acceptance rate of engineers to your company.

    More experience and lower acceptance rates improve the score.

  • Tools Community Size - How widely adopted are the tools being used by the company? And how active is the open community working on and with it?

Example:

Another client of ours had all of its infrastructure managed manually.

To increase the documentation-coverage and the automated-processes-coverage, it decided to adopt an infrastructure-as-code tool.

They considered Terraform and Pulumi, and ended up choosing Pulumi, in order to avoid hiring more full-time DevOps Engineers, and delegate responsibilities for infrastructure management to the developers.

It increased the documentation-coverage by the sheer fact that all of the infrastructure is now described in a Git repository.

It increased the automated-processes-coverage because every piece of new infrastructure was introduced into Git, would exist in every new environment, and would get automatically reconciled if its state drifts.

And the formula for the score (One last formula, I promise):

Note that this variable does NOT say “DevOps Engineering Talent Concentration Score”, because the assumptions are that:

  1. Every engineer on the team can take part in filling the DevOps capacity - it doesn’t have to be a specific team or person

  2. More experienced engineers require less training and support, and so consume less time for the DevOps Capacity

Example:

MeteorOps hires 7 engineers out of every 1,000 vetted.

We only vet DevOps Engineers with extensive production experience in at least two previous companies.

Our median seniority is 8 years of experience.

It means the ETCS (Engineering Talent Concentration Score) is 114.

🧠 Engineering Talent Concentration Score - The biggest leverage you can get

If you can take only one thing from this article, make it the engineering talent score.

Having a DevOps candidates pool of engineers with relevant experience, and hiring only the top percentile of that pool, is an insanely high-leverage action.

You get engineers with perspective on how to do things right, and perhaps more importantly, how to do things wrong.

Enjoying someone’s learning from successes, and learning from failures, saves your company lots of time learning the hard way.

External DevOps help can be useful, but it should be framed as a capacity and capability decision, not a way to postpone operating-model choices. A good partner reduces bottlenecks by building reusable platform patterns, documenting how the system is supposed to run, tightening delivery and runtime practices, and transferring knowledge back to the teams that will own the work later. If the engagement simply adds more hands to the same ticket queue, you may buy short-term relief while the underlying capacity problem keeps compounding. Use outside support when it is tied to a concrete outcome: stabilizing delivery, creating self-service infrastructure, improving cloud or Kubernetes operations, lowering incident load, or covering a specialist gap while you hire, train, or reorganize internally.

I’m not going to do that.

(P.S. - I’m the Marketing Director)

To Summarize

Instead of writing more words, here are all of the formulas:

I hope you find it useful!

I’m also interested in learning about how you used he formulas, and what insights you had as a result.

If you came up with new useful variables and formulas, please send it to me so I can take credit over inventing them.

It showed that platform engineers had become a manual intake layer for work that should have been automated, documented, delegated, or exposed through self-service. The visible symptom was “too many questions in Slack”; the underlying capacity problem was that routine delivery work still required a specialist to interpret, approve, or execute it.

    What changed: The teams reviewed recurring requests every week, grouped the highest-volume patterns, automated repeatable tasks, and created self-service paths for common developer needs. They also paired with key developers to move platform knowledge into product teams. The capacity gain did not come from asking DevOps engineers to work faster. It came from removing avoidable handoffs and making routine work executable without waiting for an answer in Slack.

  2. Company #2 example:

    A company with 30 developers had one DevOps engineer supporting delivery, infrastructure, and developer requests.

    Capacity signal: The DevOps engineer spent most of their time on support tickets opened by developers. As common deployment errors kept recurring, some developers began bypassing the standard deployment process to keep work moving.

That combination reduced the single-person bottleneck without immediately turning every platform problem into a full-time hiring decision.

With those caveats in place, here is the planning model for estimating DevOps capacity.

A practical way to estimate DevOps capacity

A useful way to estimate required DevOps capacity is to start with the work the platform team must absorb, then adjust for risk, complexity, and the level of self-service already in place:

Why this works as a planning model

  • The bigger the stuff to build and maintain - the more working hands you need

  • The more variations you need to support - the more working hands you need

  • The more self-service you have, the fewer hands-on interruptions you should need

Let’s dive into the ingredients of scale, complexity, and leverage.

The baseline: what “DevOps capacity” actually includes

The guiding principle here is simple: a DevOps engineer should enable delivery, not become a permanent checkpoint for every delivery task.

That means enabling teams to provision infrastructure, deploy workloads, store and process data, observe services, and recover from incidents with as little unnecessary handoff as possible. When every change still requires a DevOps engineer to approve, debug, click, or explain the same thing again, capacity is being consumed by friction rather than leverage.

DevOps = Enable ownership of the relevant stakeholders over the infrastructure, monitoring, security, architecture, data, configuration, deployment, orchestration, testing, and development.

‘DevOps Capacity’ is the time & effort invested in achieving “DevOps” as defined above.

⛰️ Scale - Size Matters

Start by defining the scale you are asking the platform to support. In capacity planning, “scale” is not only traffic volume. It also includes the number of services, environments, deployment paths, cloud accounts or projects, runtime patterns, data systems, compliance boundaries, and teams that depend on the platform.

“Michael, did you just create a recursive definition?”

Why yes of course! this is the rationale:

  1. Larger systems require more time and effort to understand, build, secure, operate, and maintain.

  2. Larger teams and client bases create more internal and external use cases to support, which increases the load on platform, infrastructure, and release processes.

To make the two types of scale above easier to discuss, I use two simple capacity models.

They are not scientific laws. They are structured ways to compare the demand created by your systems, teams, and operating model with the DevOps capacity your organization actually has:

Map the system scale and operational surface area

  • Resources Used could mean many things, some of them are: Storage volume, Number of CPU cores, Number of nodes, Memory used, etc.

  • System throughput is the work your systems process over time: user requests, scheduled jobs, batch runs, queue events, streaming workloads, and any other flow that creates operational load. Throughput matters because each flow tends to bring its own deployment risk, scaling pattern, observability requirement, failure mode, ownership boundary, and support expectation. A quiet batch job that fails every morning can consume more DevOps attention than a high-traffic service with mature dashboards, alerts, and rollback paths.

  • Instances per Service refers to the number of replicas of the services developed within your company, for example: Kubernetes Pods, serverless functions executions, etc.

A client's system scale example: 1-year-old startup

Scale: 3 AWS ECS clusters, 6 microservices, 3 main environments, 3–150 ephemeral development environments, and 6–40 container instances per environment

Approach: Infrastructure and deployments are managed with infrastructure as code. The company hired a part-time DevOps consultant to implement the initial system and train the development team to own routine changes, instead of creating a permanent dependency on the consultant for every deployment or environment issue.

Organization Scale

  • Number of Developers refers to the number of developers, and shame on you for bothering yourself with reading this line

  • Total Users refers to the number of active clients_

    Noteworthy:

    B2C will usually have more clients, with more standardized interfaces - DevOps Engineers most likely will be less involved in direct ways with client facing features.

    B2B on the other hand will usually have less clients, with more customized interfaces per client - DevOps Engineers are more involved with client-facing features through the developers._

A Client's Organization Scale Example - Healthcare Company:

Scale: 200 developers divided into teams of 4–12 people, 10 DevOps engineers and SREs, high autonomy per team, and no single standardized process for all developers

Approach: Infrastructure and deployments are managed with infrastructure as code to support “one-click environments.” The company also used a part-time DevOps consultant to implement an initial system and train the development team to take ownership of it.

Bonus: Check our availability for a call about scaling DevOps in your organization in a more gradual way using MeteorOps.

🥴 Complexity - More Options, Less Clarity

I know, I know… It looks similar to the chapter about Scale.

In this context, complexity is not only the number of systems you run. It is the number of choices engineers must make without strong defaults, and the uncertainty around which path is considered safe, supported, and maintainable. That uncertainty creates decision latency and makes it more likely that two teams solve the same problem in different, incompatible ways.

You are operating in a complex environment when an engineer knows what outcome they want, but still has to ask, “Is this how we do it here?”

So, what does complexity have to do with both the system and the organization?

  1. More complex system - More time and effort are required to map the available options, and customize (copy, paste, modify) or generalize (refactor, parameterize) solutions

  2. More complex organization - More time and effort are required to communicate, provide support, cascade initiatives through the company, and lower likelihood of initiatives getting accepted

This time I’ll present you with the formulas for complexity without drumrolls:

System Complexity

  • Number of Tools refers to any tool, either existing or custom-built, that helps build and maintain the system. More tools mean more capabilities, more potential integrations between tools, and more potential ways to achieve the same goals. (Tools have an upside as well!)

  • Number of Platforms means any platform on which you run workloads or consume resources (e.g. - AWS, Kubernetes, Linux, Jenkins). Using more platforms requires supporting more ways of running each workload or consuming each resource.

  • Number of Codebases refers to the repositories where your systems are developed and maintained. The more separate codebases you operate, the harder it becomes to keep development workflows consistent: build conventions drift, CI/CD pipelines fork, dependency upgrades happen unevenly, and release practices become harder to support at scale. A larger number of repositories does not automatically mean you need more DevOps capacity, but it does increase the value of shared templates, standards, and automation that prevent every team from reinventing the same delivery path.

  • Number of Services is the number of services developed by the developers: more services, more different units with different logic to them, which in turn creates more unique operational requirements.

To sum up, ‘System Complexity’ increases when there are more services, running on more platforms, managed by more tools, across more codebases.

A Client's System Complexity Example - Low Scale, High Complexity:

  • Complexity: The entire system was 1 service deployed on just 1 server, but was deployed using multiple deployment tools (chef, ansible, bash scripts), from multiple different repositories (about 10), with a specific set of steps required to fully set it up
  • Approach: Containerize everything, Consolidate the deployment to one docker-compose file, Consolidate the configuration and automation to one tool (ansible), Consolidate the repositories into one

Organization Complexity

  • Number of Teams - More teams mean supporting and maintaining more ways of work

  • Number of Hierarchy Levels - More middle-management layers in the organization make it more likely decisions and communication will cascade through it, and so increasing the time & effort for decision-making and communication

  • Level of Hierarchy-Reliance for Communication - Exactly the same effect, but focused on the culture of the company

🪄 Is there anything that makes DevOps capacity more efficient?

Calculating DevOps capacity is not just a headcount exercise. Done well, it exposes where delivery is actually getting stuck: repeated support requests, fragile release paths, manual environment provisioning, unclear ownership, noisy incident handoffs, and the morale cost of constant interruption.

The better planning question is not “how many DevOps engineers do we need?” It is “which constraint should the next unit of capacity remove?” In many organizations, adding another person to absorb tickets only makes the bottleneck quieter for a while. The higher-leverage move may be self-service environment creation, paved-road CI/CD templates, standardized cloud and Kubernetes defaults, documented escalation paths, workable access flows, or clearer ownership boundaries that show when a product team can act independently and when platform help is required. If the discussion is stuck in anecdotes, a structured DevOps maturity assessment can give teams a shared language for deciding what to automate, what to standardize, what to delegate, and where specialist DevOps or platform engineering capacity still matters. The goal is not to keep the platform team busy. It is to make the same capacity support more teams, safer releases, and faster recovery without turning that team into the permanent approval queue for every deployment, pipeline change, cloud request, access issue, or post-incident follow-up.

Valid question! And this is the formula for DevOps ‘Leverage’:

  • Documentation Coverage - Out of the internal company’s tools and processes, what percentage has documentation?

  • Automated Processes Coverage - Out of the manual processes used by the developers, what percentage was automated?

  • Engineering Talent Concentration Score - The seniority (relevant experience) of your engineering team, divided by the acceptance rate of engineers to your company.

    More experience and lower acceptance rates improve the score.

  • Tools Community Size - How widely adopted are the tools being used by the company? And how active is the open community working on and with it?

Example:

Another client of ours had all of its infrastructure managed manually.

To increase the documentation-coverage and the automated-processes-coverage, it decided to adopt an infrastructure-as-code tool.

They considered Terraform and Pulumi, and ended up choosing Pulumi, in order to avoid hiring more full-time DevOps Engineers, and delegate responsibilities for infrastructure management to the developers.

It increased the documentation-coverage by the sheer fact that all of the infrastructure is now described in a Git repository.

It increased the automated-processes-coverage because every piece of new infrastructure was introduced into Git, would exist in every new environment, and would get automatically reconciled if its state drifts.

And the formula for the score (One last formula, I promise):

Note that this variable does NOT say “DevOps Engineering Talent Concentration Score”, because the assumptions are that:

  1. Every engineer on the team can take part in filling the DevOps capacity - it doesn’t have to be a specific team or person

  2. More experienced engineers require less training and support, and so consume less time for the DevOps Capacity

Example:

We only vet DevOps Engineers with extensive production experience in at least two previous companies.

Our median seniority is 8 years of experience.

It means the ETCS (Engineering Talent Concentration Score) is 114.

If you can take only one thing from this article, make it the engineering talent score.
